essence: A library in a night train’s spare compartment brings books within reach of Alder Valley readers who miss daytime opening hours.
brief: For six Thursdays, librarian Ada Finch and local volunteers lent books from the last train through the Alder Valley. Using a journey the railway already made let them meet readers on their way home from late shifts. The trial recorded 84 loans, but keeping the service alive through winter depends on station stops, space on the train and a paid evening shift.
understanding: Finch started with a practical question about collecting a reserved book after work. Three village platforms lay on an evening train route people already used. Putting books there changed when and where people could reach a library without requiring a new journey.

The volunteers recorded 84 loans across six Thursdays. Of those loans, 31 went to people who said daytime visits were difficult. Small changes mattered too. Arranging reservations in platform order made a short, rain-swept stop easier to use.

The ledger counts loans, so a returning household may appear several times. The answer about daytime access was optional. Even if demand holds up, the railway has yet to guarantee the compartment or every winter stop, and Finch wants a paid shift before extending the route.
